html:
A Norse settlement at the northern tip of Newfoundland, Canada, the only confirmed site of Europeans in the Americas before Columbus. Tree rings in wood cut with metal tools show that Norse people were working there in 1021.

Helge Ingstad and the archaeologist Anne Stine Ingstad found the site in 1960. They dug up the remains of eight buildings of turf over wooden frames, like those in Iceland and Greenland. Finds include a bronze cloak pin, iron rivets and a spindle whorl, which shows that women were there too.

The camp was probably a base for exploring further south, used for only a few years. It matches the Vinland of the Icelandic sagas, which tell how Leif Erikson, son of Erik the Red, sailed west around the year 1000. The sagas also tell of fights with local people. The Norse did not stay, and their voyages left no lasting mark on the Americas. The site is part of the story of Viking expansion and became a World Heritage Site in 1978.
